indian-startups-a7393ac399.headline: MeitY unveils DEPA handbook to enable trusted data sharing for AI training
indian-startups-a7393ac399.fulltext:
The handbook outlines a techno-legal framework that allows institutions to collaborate on data for AI training while keeping control of their data.
The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has launched a handbook on Data Empowerment and Protection Architecture (DEPA) for AI training, an official release said Saturday.
The handbook outlines a techno-legal framework that allows institutions to collaborate on data for AI training while keeping control of their data.
IT Secretary S Krishnan unveiled the handbook, which was developed with support from the iSPIRT Foundation, at a roundtable in Bengaluru.
"The framework combines contractual permissions, controlled computing environments and privacy-enhancing safeguards. It also incorporates data provenance, enabling the origin, permissions and use of data to be traced throughout the training process, supporting accountability and transparency," the release said.
As AI becomes central to economic and social development, access to diverse, high-quality data is critical.
Yet concerns around privacy, confidentiality, intellectual property and institutional control often limit data sharing, the release said adding DEPA training addresses these challenges.
"India's AI ambitions must be matched by the ability to use data responsibly and securely," Krishnan said, adding that MeitY is committed to taking the framework forward.
Principal Scientific Adviser Ajay Kumar Sood explained that under DEPA, the model travels to the data rather than the reverse.
He said this enables multi-party and cross-border collaboration, and described DEPA as India's contribution to global science diplomacy.
The roundtable drew representatives from government, industry, academia, research among other stakeholders.

OpenAI raises just $11 billion of its $30 billion target as big investors lose their AI appetite
OpenAI raised less than half of its $30 billion fundraising target in its latest round. The company has secured about $11 billion so far, according to the Wall Street Journal. Its valuation landed at $1.25 trillion, short of the $1.4 trillion it was aiming for. The gap reportedly comes down to fading interest from major investors amid a tech sell-off driven by weak quarterly results from Google, Amazon, and Intel. OpenAI now plans to raise up to $20 billion from family offices and high-net-worth individuals. The company is reportedly planning an IPO early next year.
Rival Anthropic has been growing revenue faster lately and could go public as early as November. A strong IPO could leave Anthropic with well over $100 billion in capital to weather any rough stretch ahead. OpenAI has clawed back some market share recently, but the competition goes back and forth. OpenAI especially has been pushing hard with price cuts and more efficient models to hold its ground.

indian-startups-e6a2a984f5.headline: India Can Build Rockets, But Can Its VCs Fund The Next One?
indian-startups-e6a2a984f5.fulltext: On July 18, 2026, Skyroot Aerospace achieved a historic milestone when its Vikram-1 rocket successfully placed satellites into orbit, becoming the first privately developed Indian rocket to accomplish an orbital launch. For a country whose space programme was historically dominated by ISRO, it was a powerful demonstration of what Indian entrepreneurs could achieve in advanced technology. Three months later, Ashlee Vance — the American journalist best known for his bestselling biography of Elon Musk and reporting on the global space industry — turned his attention to India's technological ambitions. His question was less about the capabilities of Indian engineers than the willingness of Indian investors to back them. He asked: "Why are Indian VCs so afraid to take risk and make money?" The October 22 post accompanied Vance's Core Memory feature exploring India's emerging hardware economy. After three weeks meeting 15 Indian companies, Vance appeared impressed by the technological ambitions of their founders but far less enthusiastic about the state of the country's venture capital ecosystem. He subsequently doubled down, claiming he had rarely encountered a market where VCs had a worse reputation among founders. What followed was an unusually candid debate. Founders complained about investors demanding commercial traction before technologies had been validated, prolonged diligence processes and excessive dependence on founder pedigree. Investors pushed back, highlighting India's growing list of deeptech successes, the increasing availability of specialist capital and the structural challenges of financing scientific innovation. But the timing makes this debate far more consequential than another disagreement on X. As AI threatens to automate parts of the software-services industry that helped establish India as a global technology powerhouse, the country's ability to create and own foundational technologies is becoming increasingly important. India has demonstrated that its entrepreneurs can build complex technologies. The more difficult question is whether venture capital and private equity can repeatedly back such breakthroughs. Indian Founders Aren't Just Questioning Capital, They're Questioning The VCs One of the strongest responses came from Akash Kulgod, founder of Dognosis, which is developing canine-assisted cancer detection technology. In a detailed post, Kulgod compared his experience interacting with approximately 80 investors, around 65% of whom were based in the US. His criticism ran deeper than simply stating that Indian VCs rejected his startup. He said US investors typically made relatively quick decisions, rejecting the opportunity when they lacked conviction in the technology or founding team. Some Indian investors, he alleged, extended discussions over repeated meetings and visits, only to demand commercial traction or stop responding. For a company developing medical technology, any delays in the development cycle hurt. Clinical validation, technical testing and regulatory approvals can require years before meaningful commercial revenue becomes possible. An investor demanding revenue before the technology is proven may effectively eliminate the opportunity instead of properly evaluating the technology. Kulgod also questioned whether some investors possessed the technical understanding needed to assess unfamiliar scientific problems. Other founders raised concerns about investor dependence on IIT or IIM credentials, professional networks and the reputations of existing backers when evaluating early-stage startups. These are undoubtedly individual accounts, not evidence that such practices are universal across Indian VC firms. But they expose an uncomfortable question. If investors require commercial traction, institutional validation and another investor's conviction before writing a cheque, how much technological risk are they actually underwriting? There is an important difference between financing a technology after it works and financing the experiment that determines whether it can work. Deeptech needs both. And as the experience of several founders in India shows, the latter remains one of the most difficult investment decisions. The Numbers Show A Funding Surge, But Are More Founders Benefiting? According to Inc42 DataLabs, Indian deeptech startups raised approximately $500 Mn across 87 deals in 2025. The sector emerged as one of the most active by deal count, but its funding remained substantially below fintech's $2.5 Bn, enterprise tech's $1.8 Bn and ecommerce's $1.7 Bn. The latest quarterly figures, however, suggest that investor preferences are changing. In Q3 2026, deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 funding deals, compared with $105 Mn across 29 deals in the year-ago quarter. Funding surged 176% YoY, dramatically outpacing the broader startup ecosystem's 5% growth. Deeptech funding nearly tripled, but the number of funded deals actually declined. Pixxel's $100 Mn funding round alone accounted for approximately one-third of the deeptech capital deployed during the quarter. Bengaluru captured around 65% of the sector's funding. At the broader ecosystem level, investors also wrote larger seed cheques to fewer companies. Early stage funding fell 18% YoY to $164 Mn across 93 deals, even as the median cheque size increased 20% to $1.2 Mn. The contrast with the first half of 2026 is instructive. According to Inc42's H1 2026 funding report, advanced hardware and technology startups raised $365 Mn across a record 66 deals, reflecting an 18% rise in funding and a 53% jump in deal volume. That suggests improving breadth of investment during the first half, followed by greater concentration in the third quarter. There’s no trend to explore here, but this disparity demonstrates why headline funding growth is an insufficient measure of access to capital. Larger investments are increasingly flowing towards a smaller pool of technically validated companies. So the deeper question is whether more first-time founders pursuing unproven technologies are securing their first institutional cheques, which strikes at the heart of what Vance was saying. Are India's VCs Backing Convenience Over Breakthroughs? A separate debate over India's startup funding priorities had already exposed a fundamental divide between founders and investors over where venture capital should flow. In an October 17 post on X, Neosapien founder Dhananjay Yadav questioned why consumer-service startups burning substantial amounts of capital could attract large investments, while deeptech companies generating higher revenues with lower cash burn struggled to raise even a fraction of that money. Responding to Yadav, Untitled Ventures' Anmol Maini made a provocative claim that much of deeptech could eventually prove to be a "grift", arguing that quick commerce and on-demand services might contribute more to the economy. Blume Ventures partner Arpit Agarwal offered an explanation rooted in investment economics. Investment capital, he argued, gravitates towards opportunities offering lower perceived risk or disproportionately higher returns. The distinction to note here is that the economic importance of a technology and its attractiveness as a venture investment are not necessarily the same thing. This is consistent with concerns Agarwal had raised in an earlier interview with Inc42, where he explained why capital-intensive original equipment manufacturing (OEM) businesses are often poorly suited to conventional early-stage VC financing. Pixxel founder Awais Ahmed, however, challenged the notion that consumer internet and deeptech should be competing for relevance and the same pie of venture capital. In a detailed post, Ahmed argued that they represent different layers of the same technological economy. A ten-minute grocery delivery depends on decades of breakthroughs in semiconductors, GPS, lithium-ion batteries, cellular networks and computing — technologies developed long before their commercial applications became apparent. Consumer businesses make technology accessible at scale. Deeptech expands what technology can achieve. Ahmed acknowledged that successful internet companies create wealth that can eventually be reinvested into deeptech. But foundational technologies cannot simply be treated as investments to pursue once quicker commercial opportunities have been exhausted. Developing competitive capabilities in semiconductors, aerospace, advanced materials or energy requires years of research, specialised talent, experimentation and industrial infrastructure. And therein lies India’s venture capital allocation dilemma. The country has spent the past decade building a thriving consumer internet economy. But its ambition to emerge as a global technology powerhouse will require investing in foundational technologies long before their commercial returns become predictable. The Criticism Ignores How Far India Has Come Unacademy cofounder Gaurav Munjal was among the prominent voices challenging Vance. In a response on X, Munjal described the assessment as dated and rage-baiting. He pointed to Astrobase, Airbound and Sarvam AI as examples of ambitious companies successfully raising capital, while highlighting the outcomes achieved by Groww, Eternal and Meesho. His broader argument was that India's VC ecosystem had improved dramatically, and that fintech and digital commerce remained important opportunities given the size of the domestic market. Ather Energy attracted early support from IIT Madras-linked programmes, the Flipkart founders, Tiger Global and Hero MotoCorp before eventually becoming a listed company. Skyroot has achieved orbital launch capability. Agnikul has demonstrated indigenous launch technology. Pixxel is developing hyperspectral satellites, while Airbound is attempting to commercialise autonomous aircraft. Munjal’s point was that these achievements challenge the idea that India lacks investors willing to finance complex technologies. Nevertheless, several high-profile deeptech startups have relied significantly on overseas capital. Airbound's $37 Mn Series A, for instance, was led by US-based Greenoaks. An Indian startup's ability to attract international investors is a sign of some success for the company, but it does not necessarily establish that domestic investors are equally willing to finance such technologies. Still, Munjal's argument gains weight from his own next move. Along with Unacademy cofounder Roman Saini, he is raising a ₹700 Cr fund called Longshot Capital, targeting AI, manufacturing, robotics, spacetech and defence. It represents a growing pattern: founders who created wealth and operating expertise through India's first startup generation are increasingly attempting to finance its next. Indian VCs Have Avoided Real Venture Risk, But That Is Changing Antler India partner Nitin Sharma offered one of the more balanced assessments. In a detailed October 24 post, Sharma acknowledged that India's venture ecosystem had historically failed to generate consistent venture-scale returns partly because investors avoided genuine venture risk. But he argued that the situation had begun changing. Sharma identified two categories of founders increasingly receiving backing: the first being experienced technologists and academics, and the second category covering young, unconventional self-taught entrepreneurs. Sharma said Antler had acted as the first institutional believer in 10 deeptech ventures since 2022. india-deep-tech-4125b70c2e.fulltext:

Coratia Technologies raises ₹18 crore funding led by MGF Kavachh
Underwater robotics startup Coratia Technologies has raised ₹18 crore in a bridge round led by MGF Kavachh to execute its ₹66 crore Indian Navy programme, strengthen research and development, and scale manufacturing and deployment.
The latest round follows a ₹17 crore pre-series A round in 2025, backed by MGF Kavachh, Piper and SIDBI.
Founded by Debendra Pradhan and Biswajit Swain, Coratia develops remotely operated underwater vehicles (ROVs) and robotic systems for defence, industrial inspection and critical infrastructure.
The new capital will go towards the Navy programme, strengthening core underwater robotics capabilities and building the manufacturing and deployment capacity required to serve defence and industrial customers.
The ₹66 crore Indian Navy contract, signed in September 2025, covers the supply and maintenance of indigenous underwater robotic systems for ship-hull cleaning, minor salvage operations and the inspection of submerged infrastructure.
“We are building a technology platform that can evolve with India’s requirements. Indian waters present unique challenges, including high turbidity, silt, low visibility and changing currents. Our focus is on miniaturising technology while advancing our systems’ intelligence, capability and deployability across defence, infrastructure and industrial applications,” said Debendra Pradhan, co-founder and CEO, Coratia Technologies.
MGF Kavachh had invested in Coratia before it secured the Navy order. For Raj Sethia, founder and managing partner at MGF Kavachh, the follow-on investment reflects a conviction built through working with the company over roughly a year and a half, rather than a decision based solely on the contract.
“The Navy contract was a milestone we expected them to achieve, given the quality of work they were doing even before our first investment. This round is about backing that same conviction, which has only grown stronger with time,” Sethia told ETEntrepreneur.
Building for difficult underwater conditions
Coratia’s origins date back to 2014, when its founders were students at NIT Rourkela participating in robotics competitions in India and overseas. During that period, co-founder and CTO Biswajit Swain said they identified a gap in underwater inspection, where operations continued to depend heavily on human divers despite the risks involved.
“People are still using manual divers to carry out any kind of inspection work, and we all know how hazardous the underwater condition is,” he told ETEntrepreneur. “Most of the infrastructure remains uninspected.”
Swain said platform stability is critical to underwater inspection, as excessive movement in strong currents can affect image clarity and an ROV’s ability to identify objects. Coratia’s engineering approach focuses on maintaining stability while carrying out complex inspection tasks.
Coratia’s platforms combine acoustic sensors, multibeam sonar, Doppler velocity logs (DVL) and ultra-short baseline (USBL) navigation systems with cameras and specialised inspection payloads. Depending on the configuration, these can include robotic manipulators and thickness gauges used to inspect ferrous materials. JalaSimha is designed for operations at depths of up to 300 metres.
Swain highlighted platform stability as a key technical consideration. A vehicle that moves excessively in strong currents can struggle to capture clear images or identify underwater objects, undermining the usefulness of the inspection data. Coratia’s focus, he said, is on combining manoeuvrability with the stability required for complex inspection tasks.
Its longer-term goal is to increase indigenous component content and reduce dependence on externally integrated solutions. The company says its compact, lightweight ROVs are designed to accommodate multiple capabilities without compromising manoeuvrability in difficult underwater environments.
Beyond the Navy contract
Coratia’s customer and partner base includes the Indian Navy, Indian Oil, Indian Railways, Tata Steel, Hindalco, SAIL, Neelachal Ispat Nigam, Jindal Steel and Power, and NIT Rourkela. Its systems can be used to inspect dams and reservoirs, ports, bridges, pipelines, offshore assets, ship infrastructure and subsea communication networks.
“Our work extends well beyond the Navy programme,” Swain said. “We continue to invest in autonomy, sensing, navigation, underwater perception and intervention capabilities.”
For MGF Kavachh, the potential to expand across sectors is central to the investment case. Sethia said the fund focuses on Indian companies addressing strategic problems linked to technological self-reliance, including in defence, aerospace, critical communications, semiconductors and critical materials.
“Long-term sustainability and scale come from industry-level applications,” Sethia said, adding that portfolio companies should be able to serve multiple customers and markets. “They're not competing on margin by assembling things which anybody else could do. Some intellectual property is being built and gone behind it.”
The venture fund also works with other capital providers to help companies navigate funding needs when development milestones take longer than expected.
For Coratia, the immediate challenge is translating its technology into repeatable, deployment-ready products. Underwater robotics requires mechanical engineering, electronics, sensing, navigation, and control systems to function reliably together in demanding conditions. Extensive testing and iteration are needed to validate performance at depth, in poor visibility, and around submerged structures.

health-tech-6d13e8f8dd.headline: EXCLUSIVE: India orders Sun Pharma to halt eye-care drug production at plant after quality lapses
health-tech-6d13e8f8dd.fulltext:
[Text below is Business Today's report of the same story — the original outlet blocks automated reading. The link still points to the original.]
Sun Pharma's Assam facility ordered to halt production
The Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation and the office of the Drugs Controller Assam ordered the shutdown after a joint central-state inspection identified lapses in systems intended to ensure product quality and safety.
The action prevents Sun Pharma, India's biggest pharmaceutical company, from resuming ophthalmic drug production at the facility until regulators accept its compliance report. The company had previously said the Assam site was expected to become one of its largest manufacturing hubs for sterile products, a business it has identified as a key global growth driver.
The regulators had issued a show-cause notice to Sun Pharma on August 10, citing failures in the quality management system, the documents showed. Dissatisfied with the company's response, they ordered a halt to the manufacturing, sale and distribution of all ophthalmic products from the facility.
Regulators seek details of 332 recalled batches
The regulators sought more information about the recall of 332 batches of ophthalmic suspension products, which are liquids used to treat eye conditions.
In an internal notice sent to stockists at the time, Sun Pharma said it was withdrawing the products as a "precautionary measure." The company did not publicly disclose details of the recall.
A company compliance report submitted in response to the order is being reviewed by the regulator, an official familiar with the matter told Reuters. The official declined to be identified because they were not authorised to speak to the media.
"We voluntarily initiated a temporary cessation of manufacturing activities and informed the regulators," Sun Pharma said in a statement on Friday, adding that remedial measures had been put in place.
The company did not respond to a request for comment on the recall. It says on its website that it follows a single global quality standard.
Recall could involve hundreds of thousands of bottles
The recalled products included Lotepred 1% 5ml eye drops, Nepalact OD eye drops, Nepalact-Z, Brinzotim eye drops 5ml and Depopred 2ml. According to doctors, the drops are used to treat eye inflammation, infections and chronic eye diseases.
Based on product packaging, most of the recalled products were manufactured at the Assam facility in Kokjhar village. Reuters could not independently verify whether the 332 batches cited by regulators were related only to the 11 brands identified in the recall notice or included additional brands.
The affected batches could amount to hundreds of thousands of eye-drop bottles, according to industry experts who declined to be identified because they were not authorised to speak publicly.
Ophthalmology contributes about 3% of Sun Pharma's domestic revenue, according to its 2025-26 annual report. It is also one of the company's key areas in the US.
Sun Pharma reported a fall in second-quarter profit on Friday, weighed down by a one-time charge related to its acquisition of US-based Organon.
Patient-safety advisory flagged Predmet eye drops
The recall coincided with a patient-safety advisory issued in June by the All India Ophthalmological Society, an independent body of eye specialists. The advisory warned that certain batches of Predmet eye drops appeared to be contaminated.
"There were some adverse cases of infections reported in patients who used Predmet and we got sealed bottles investigated and found it was contaminated," Santosh Honavar, a doctor and secretary of AIOS, told the news agency. He added that Sun Pharma had also recalled those Predmet drops.
Sun Pharma did not respond to a request for comment on the AIOS advisory.
Indian drug quality standards face scrutiny
Indian regulators did not respond to requests for comment, and the regulatory agency did not issue a public health alert after the recall.
India's drug quality standards have faced increased scrutiny at home and overseas in recent years after locally manufactured cough syrups were linked to the deaths of children in India and countries including Gambia and Uzbekistan.
This is not the first time Sun Pharma's sterile manufacturing facilities have faced regulatory scrutiny. Last year, the US Food and Drug Administration halted shipments from the company's Halol plant in Gujarat after inspectors cited shortcomings in contamination controls.
Sun Pharma's Assam facility will remain unable to manufacture ophthalmic drugs until regulators accept its compliance report. The company has said it voluntarily stopped manufacturing activities and implemented remedial measures, while the scale and impact of the recall involving 332 batches of eye-care products remain unclear.

india-006cc571a7.headline: India-Bangladesh Ganga water treaty renewal in doubt as December deadline nears
india-006cc571a7.fulltext:
Significant changes to the treaty terms, including a much shorter tenure, are also being considered, it is learnt. The 30-year-old treaty, signed in 1996, will lapse on December 12.
India is unlikely to renew the treaty automatically without a visit by Rahman, sources indicated.
The treaty is crucial as it manages the sharing of the Ganges River waters with Bangladesh during the lean season from January 1 to May 31 every year - controlled through the water flow from Farakka Barrage in Murshidabad West Bengal- just 20 kms upstream of Bangladesh.
However, several Indian stakeholders have sought that the treaty be renegotiated to adequately address sharply increasing demand for fresh water from Bihar to West Bengal besides growing industrial needs and thermal power plants.
Bihar Chief Minister Samrat Chaudhary on Friday stressed that the state's interests must be protected before the international treaty with Bangladesh is renewed.
There are also calls for modifying the treaty to bring in a more comprehensive river basin approach that addresses concerns like heavy siltation around the Farakka barrage that impacts water flow in adjoining areas.
The treaty, however, is a political hot button issue in Bangladesh.
The ruling Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) has been pitching that the 'minimum guarantee' clause of the 1977 bilateral agreement - which ensured Bangladesh got 80% of its scheduled water allocation in the lean period - be restored.
It further argues that the 1996 Treaty framework inked under the Sheikh Hasina led Awami League does not protect Bangladesh's agricultural interests adequately and there is a need to break from this template.
The 1996 treaty allows for 50:50 water sharing between the two countries when water flow drops to 70,000 cusecs or less while when it drops even below 70,000, Bangladesh gets a fixed 35,000 cusecs. In effect, both countries are guaranteed 35,000 cusecs of water in alternating three 10-day periods between March 11 and May 10 every year.
However, with the kind of changes being sought by the BNP in Bangladesh and the sharply increasing water demand within India, the continuation of the treaty in existing form has become challenging.
Much hinges now on the Bangladesh PM's visit.
Since his election early this year, there were at least four occasions when PM Tarique Rahman's visit was planned but a section of establishment in Dhaka sabotaged the plan on the pretext of Sheikh Hasina's extradition. The radical Jamaat-e-Islami has been trying to influence Rahman government's India policy and pushing for an anti-India narrative. A section of the establishment in Dhaka has raised anti-India rhetoric, forcing the PM to go slow while engaging with New Delhi. There's desperation in some quarters in Dhaka about Rahman's visit focusing Ganges Treaty renewal.

climate-energy-c8aa6bba07.headline: India's Energy Storage Capacity Must Expand 7.6 Times By FY32: CareEdge

India's Energy Storage Capacity Must Expand 7.6 Times By FY32: CareEdge
Updated: Oct 31, 2026 01:21:26pm
India's Energy Storage Capacity Must Expand 7.6 Times By FY32: CareEdge
New Delhi, Oct 31 (KNN) India will need to add 357.4 gigawatt-hours (GWh) of energy storage capacity over the next six years to support its expanding renewable energy sector, according to a report by CareEdge.
The country's operational storage capacity stood at around 54 GWh as of June 2026, against a projected requirement of 411.4 GWh by FY32 under the Central Electricity Authority's (CEA) National Electricity Plan.
This means India's storage infrastructure will need to expand nearly 7.6 times from its June 2026 level to meet the projected requirement.
The gap assumes significance as renewable energy capacity continues to grow, increasing the need for infrastructure to store surplus electricity and supply it during periods of peak demand, the report noted.
Battery And Pumped Storage Requirements
Non-fossil sources accounted for 54.18 per cent of India's installed electricity generation capacity as of June 2026, surpassing fossil fuel-based capacity. However, coal continues to account for the majority of actual electricity generation, reported Money Control.
According to the National Electricity Plan, India's storage requirement by FY32 comprises 236.22 GWh from battery energy storage systems (BESS) and 175.18 GWh from pumped storage projects.
The government has estimated investments of around Rs 3.49 lakh crore in battery storage and Rs 1.29 lakh crore in pumped storage by FY32, taking the combined projected investment requirement to approximately Rs 4.78 lakh crore.
Grid Infrastructure Emerges As Key Challenge
CareEdge-ESG noted that India's renewable energy expansion is creating investment opportunities beyond generation capacity, particularly in energy storage, transmission infrastructure and grid modernisation.
The rapid addition of renewable energy projects has also increased pressure on the country's electricity transmission network, the report said.
Unlike conventional thermal power plants, solar and wind installations cannot generate electricity continuously. The challenge is therefore shifting from simply expanding renewable generation capacity to ensuring that electricity can be stored, transmitted and supplied reliably.
CareEdge-ESG identified transmission infrastructure as one of the major gaps in India's energy transition, noting that grid development has struggled to keep pace with renewable capacity additions.
Storage Crucial To 500 GW Target
With India targeting 500 GW of non-fossil electricity capacity by 2030, expanding energy storage infrastructure will be critical to integrating intermittent renewable power into the grid.
The development of storage, transmission and modern grid systems will help translate the country's renewable capacity expansion into reliable electricity supply and greater utilisation of clean energy.

deep-tech-b48592f777.headline: ISRO Chief Explains How NVS-03 Succeeded In Expanding NavIC
deep-tech-b48592f777.fulltext:
ISRO Chief Explains How NVS-03 Succeeded In Expanding NavIC
The NVS-03 mission has restored India’s regional navigation satellite system NavIC’s minimum operational configuration of four satellites.
Sriharikota: The successful launch of navigation satellite NVS-03 has strengthened India’s indigenous NavIC system, with Isro incorporating changes that addressed the technical problem encountered during the NVS-02 mission in January 2025. Addressing media at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, SHAR, in the early hours of Saturday after the successful launch of GSLV-F18, Isro chairman Dr V. Narayanan said the space agency had kept three pyro valves open in NVS-03 to prevent a recurrence of the problem encountered during the launch of its predecessor.
The precaution followed detailed technical assessment, including vibration and shock tests, by a national-level committee headed by former Isro chairman A.S. Kiran Kumar. In January 2025, NVS-02 could not be manoeuvred into its intended operational orbit after an electrical signal failed to reach a pyro valve in the oxidiser line of its propulsion system.
The subsequent investigation identified a possible connector-contact issue in the electrical circuit. Isro incorporated changes in NVS-03 to prevent the problem from recurring.
Dr Narayanan said GSLV-F18 has injected with high accuracy the 2,250-kg satellite into its designated Geosynchronous Transfer Orbit (GTO). The planned perigee of 170.36 km has been achieved at 170.31 km, while the planned apogee of 37,247 km is 38,080 km.
He described the orbital injection accuracy as one of the best performances by a launch vehicle. The NVS-03 mission has restored India’s regional navigation satellite system NavIC (Navigation with Indian Constellation)’s minimum operational configuration of four satellites. The system provides Position, Navigation, and Timing (PNT) services across India as well as in an area extending approximately 1,500 km beyond the mainland. Highlighting NavIC’s applications, the Isro chairman said around 10,400 locomotives and 64,000 fishing vessels are being tracked in real time using the system. The agency aims to extend the tracking facility to one lakh fishing vessels within the next six months under the Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana. Around 15 lakh vehicles have also been fitted with tracking devices. Dr Narayanan said the introduction of L1 civilian navigation signal in NVS-03, alongside the existing L5 and S-band signals; would expand the scope of NavIC applications. Wider compatibility with civilian mobile phones, however, would depend on strengthening the constellation to its full seven-satellite configuration. The Isro chairman disclosed that the next-generation navigation satellites NVS-04 and NVS-05 are to be launched within approximately 10 months. Their deployment is expected to improve the continuity, accuracy, and reliability of India’s navigation services. The NVS-03 mission is testimony to a shorter launch schedule.
The launch campaign had been completed in 47 days, while GSLV-F18 took off 56 days after the previous GSLV mission. The four L40 strap-on boosters had been readied in 37 days, reflecting Isro’s efforts to increase launch frequency and operational efficiency. Dr Narayanan said Isro is preparing for five more launches before the end of the current financial year.
These include the first un-crewed Gaganyaan mission G1, two PSLV missions, a small satellite mission, and a private launch. Those present at the press briefing included senior Isro officials Thomas Kurian, GSLV-F18 Mission director, and U.P. Rajeev, Vikram Sarabhai Space Centre director. ai-d66aef25de.headline: Anthropic's watermark rollout leaves a loophole on two older Claude models
ai-d66aef25de.fulltext:
Anthropic's watermark rollout leaves a loophole on two older Claude models
Anthropic is expanding its text watermark to four more Claude models, but API users can dodge the mark on two of them by tweaking a single sampling parameter.
In an email to API customers, Anthropic said it will watermark Claude Mythos 5, Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Opus 4.6, and Claude Sonnet 4.6. Newer models like Claude Opus 5.5 already carry the mark, and the rollout on Amazon Bedrock may take a few extra days.
Anthropic calls the watermark an "imperceptible pattern in word choice" that doesn't change meaning, quality, or readability. The company says it adds no extra characters or tokens, doesn't affect pricing or request and response formats, and barely slows output speed. Anthropic also says the watermark "contains no information about the user, their organization, or their conversations with Claude."
Anthropic applies the watermark only at default settings on two older models
On Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6, Anthropic says the watermark kicks in only when developers leave the three sampling parameters at their default values. Those parameters, temperature, top_p, and top_k, control how much randomness the model uses when picking words. A minor tweak to any one of them is enough to dodge the watermark. Anthropic warns in its email that "If you rely on the watermark for your own compliance, keep these settings at their defaults."
The email doesn't mention that caveat for Claude Mythos 5 or Claude Opus 4.7, which suggests the watermark applies to those models regardless of sampling settings. But the loophole on the older models is still notable, since Opus 4.6 remains Anthropic's best writing model, ahead of even Opus 5.5.
Anthropic has a detection API in private preview for verifying the watermark and offers more details on its content labeling information page.
Anthropic retrofits older Claude models to meet the EU AI Act deadline
Anthropic points to the EU AI Act's December deadline as the reason it's watermarking older models now. Every model released after Aug. 2, 2026, shipped with the watermark on day one, while older models are getting it in stages. Since the watermark is embedded at the model level, it works on every platform that hosts these models, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry. Customers can't turn it off.
Anthropic uses a variant of Google DeepMind's SynthID text method, which tweaks the randomness behind word selection to produce a statistically detectable pattern. OpenAI launched its own watermarking system textGrain in October 2026, but it only activates by default for ChatGPT and Codex users in the EU. API customers worldwide can flip it on or off, and it ships disabled. Google Deepmind open-sourced SynthID for text and built it into the Gemini models.
Whether watermarking truly leaves text quality untouched is disputed. Blogger John Gruber argues that no two synonyms mean exactly the same thing, so picking words by a watermark key instead of semantic fit inevitably degrades precision. The legal trade outlet Artificial Lawyer raises a separate concern for law firms, where clients who've banned AI use could discover the mark, and multiple watermarks layered inside one document could create complications.

ai-2c75f48ca2.headline: Google Deepmind creates a global map of forests with satellite data and AI
ai-2c75f48ca2.fulltext:
Google Deepmind creates a global map of forests with satellite data and AI
Key Points
- Google Deepmind and the World Resources Institute created a global satellite map of 2020 land cover, classifying areas at 10-meter resolution into six categories, including primary forest, plantations, and tree crops.
- The system uses AlphaEarth Foundations and multiple image-recognition stages to distinguish forest types by growth and harvest cycles, not appearance alone.
- The map achieved 90.2% overall accuracy and outperformed European Commission maps on the same test data, but identified only about half of tree crops and planted forests and 60% of plantations.
Google Deepmind and the World Resources Institute have developed ForTy, an AI map that distinguishes primary forests, timber plantations, and tree crop farms worldwide.
Satellite maps usually show whether trees grow in a given area without identifying the forest or crop type. ForTy, short for Forest Typology, goes further by assigning the world's land area in 2020 to 6 classes at 10-meter resolution. These cover primary forest, naturally regenerating forest, planted forest, plantation forest, tree crops such as oil palm, rubber, or cocoa, and other land. The authors say ForTy is the first global map of its kind. Earlier datasets, including one from the European Commission, cover only parts of the world.
EU deforestation rules need a reliable 2020 reference point
The main driver behind the project is the EU Regulation on Deforestation-free Products (EUDR), which prohibits goods linked to forests cleared or degraded after December 31, 2020, including goods produced after primary forest was converted to a plantation. Oil palm and cocoa farms count as agricultural land, so companies assessing supply chain risks need to know how a site was used in 2020.
ForTy gives them that 2020 reference point and could also feed into other initiatives that depend on the same kind of data, including the Tropical Forest Forever Facility (TFFF) and the UN goal of protecting 30 percent of the world's land by 2030.
Building that reference point is hard because a forest's type depends on its history, not just how it looks, DeepMind says. An old planted mixed forest can look like a natural one from space, and a recently cleared plantation still counts as forest by definition even though satellite images show bare ground.
ForTy uses three model stages to refine its classifications
To distinguish these categories, ForTy runs on Google DeepMind's AlphaEarth Foundations model, which compresses data from multiple satellites into a compact description of each pixel. Several image recognition models build on those descriptions, starting with one that learns from verified examples.
That first model's predictions, combined with outside data on tree heights, buildings, and forest loss, become expanded training data for a second model. A final step analyzes several years of data together to smooth outliers. Google's Gemini language model also helped adapt older training data to the EU's definitions.
During those correction rounds, experts added about 43,000 examples to address errors such as vineyards in Europe classified as tree crops, natural pine forests in Central America labeled as planted forests, and oil palms missed in Africa and Indonesia.
Even with those corrections, some distinctions remain out of reach for satellites alone. Satellite images rarely show how land is managed, so the researchers use a 40-year rotation period to separate plantations from other planted forests, and that cutoff does not fit every region.
ForTy is less reliable for plantations and tree crops
To check the map, 2 experts reviewed each of 8,190 randomly selected sites, finding it correct in 90.2 percent of cases. The authors warn that this overall score gets a large boost from the easy-to-identify "other land" class.
Results vary sharply by forest type. The map correctly identified 89 percent of primary forests that experts confirmed on the ground but found only about half of tree crops and planted forests and 60 percent of plantations. Flipping the lens, roughly a quarter to a third of areas mapped as plantations or tree crops turned out to be misclassified, and the map was wrong for a third of areas labeled as planted forest.
These gaps hit the boundaries that matter most for the EUDR, and uncertainty in the evaluation may also make the results look slightly better than they are. Experts were most often unsure about managed areas, and the team excluded those uncertain cases from its assessment.
ForTy still outperforms European Commission maps made specifically for the EUDR on the same test data, scoring 95.5 percent compared with 93.6 percent for forest versus nonforest classification, and 90.9 percent compared with 87.8 percent for forest types.
The model also inherited a weakness from its training data, whose annotators rarely classified forests near roads or settlements as primary forest, even when the forests appeared untouched.
Sweden has plenty of trees but little natural forest
The researchers estimate that the world has about 4.1 billion hectares of forest, including nearly 3.9 billion hectares of natural forest, of which about 2 billion hectares are primary forest. Planted forests cover about 250 million hectares, and tree crops cover nearly 200 million hectares, mostly in Asia.
Regional errors complicate that picture. The map overestimates primary forest in Asia by about 200 million hectares, largely in Russia's conifer forests. In Africa, it instead misses about 94 million hectares of forest, likely because of open dry forests and savannas.
About two-thirds of Sweden's forest area is planted, and natural forest covers only around one-fifth of the country. The authors say overall tree cover there may be adequate, but the share of natural forest, which matters for biodiversity, could be critically low. The Democratic Republic of the Congo, Indonesia, and Brazil have the highest shares of natural forest.
ForTy still struggles with shaded crops and open woodlands
Beyond these regional errors, some land uses remain difficult to classify. In some regions, the map still labels shaded cocoa or coffee grown beneath a natural canopy as forest, and selectively logged or burned forests also pose problems.
ForTy does not yet have a separate class for open woodlands, which the EUDR treats separately, though the researchers say future versions should add one. Users can make their own classification choices using the dataset's confidence scores for each class, which let them set their own thresholds.
The map, classification layer, and test data are freely available under a CC BY 4.0 license, including in Google Earth Engine. Google DeepMind has released the code in the GeeFlow and JEO repositories.
Deepmind introduced the underlying AlphaEarth Foundations model in July 2025 as a kind of virtual satellite. It combines optical satellite images, radar, laser scans, and climate simulations into a compact description of each 10-by-10-meter area, with annual embeddings covering years since 2017 freely available in Google Earth Engine.
ForTy is one of the first large mapping projects built on those embeddings and, Google says, is part of Earth AI. That connection places the project within a broader effort, as Google connected Earth AI to Gemini in fall 2025 to help detect floods, droughts, and algal blooms faster.

ai-bc398a80a0.headline: Judge allows NAACP lawsuit over xAI data center pollution to move forward
ai-bc398a80a0.fulltext:
A federal judge denied a motion by xAI seeking to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit accusing the SpaceX-owned company of failing to obtain permits needed to operate the gas turbines powering its Colossus data center outside Memphis.
Suing on behalf of the NAACP, the Southern Environmental Law Center said the AI company had “installed and operated at least 35 combustion turbines and other sources of air pollution at the Colossus site without ever obtaining the necessary preconstruction or operating air permits.” It also accused xAI of violating the Clean Air Act.
xAI sought to have the lawsuit dismissed, claiming that the turbines are exempt from permitting requirements because they’re mobile. The company also argued that the plaintiffs did not have the standing to sue.
“Because the plaintiffs have statutory standing under the Clean Air Act, because the combustion turbines are not ‘mobile sources’ under Mississippi’s [State Implementation Plan], and because the citizen suit provision does not violate Article II of the Constitution or the private nondelegation doctrine, the plaintiffs’ claims will proceed,” Judge Debra M. Brown wrote in her decision.
Focusing on xAI’s claim that these kinds of citizen lawsuits are unconstitutional, Judge Brown wrote, “Because citizen suit plaintiffs sue on their own behalf, in their own name, and seek penalties that redress harm to themselves, they are not exercising the federal government’s executive power.”
TechCrunch has reached out to SpaceX for comment.
In a statement, the NAACP’s director of environmental and climate justice Abre’ Connor described this as “another important victory in our effort to hold xAI accountable.” (A similar motion to dismiss from the Department of Justice was denied earlier this month)
“The courts have repeatedly rejected attempts by xAI and the DOJ to dismiss the NAACP’s Clean Air Act case, affirming our right to pursue justice for communities impacted by pollution,” Connor said. “Our position has been clear: xAI cannot operate gas turbines without the required permits.”
The NAACP lawsuit is moving forward as public opinion seems to have turned sharply against data centers, with New York recently passing a moratorium on new data centers and other state and local governments considering similar measures.
The backlash also prompted Amazon and Microsoft to promise to stop using NDAs in their dealings with government agencies, and it could be a significant factor in the imminent U.S. midterm elections.

SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey on Saturday said the market regulator is monitoring developments relating to governance at the holding company level in the Tata Group, and pointed out that the group's listed companies and their promoters are subject to SEBI's disclosure and compliance norms.
The comments came amid differences over governance matters at Tata Sons, the group's holding company, including the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran as chairman and the question of its proposed listing.
"At the holding company level, there are some issues, as that's not really a listed company. The rest of the companies, those which are listed, follow all the LODR (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) norms," Pandey told reporters on the sidelines of the launch of the Bharat Chamber Investors Forum.
These listed companies and promoters of those firms are subject to all norms, he said.
Asked whether the SEBI was keeping track of Tata Group's developments, he said, "Yes... I mean in the sense of, you know, we have to keep monitoring all the developments."

The Tata Group has 26 publicly listed companies, with a combined market capitalisation of $328 billion as of March 31, 2025, according to its FY25 annual report.

indian-startups-0e186d1855.headline: CapGrid Secures ₹50 Cr Funding To Deepen Its Manufacturing Play
indian-startups-0e186d1855.fulltext: Delhi NCR-based B2B manufacturing startup CapGrid has raised ₹50 Cr (about $5.2 Mn) in a Pre-Series B round to develop higher-end precision components and expand into sectors such as drone manufacturing and data centres. The funding round values CapGrid at ₹430 Cr (about $45.3 Mn), cofounder and CEO Dheeraj Tiwari told Inc42. Led by Hero Enterprise Venture Partners, the investment arm of Sunil Munjal-led Hero Enterprise, it included primary and secondary transactions, with participation from Axilor Ventures, Anicut Capital, Nexus Venture Partners, and angels. Part of the primary proceeds will fund R&D into higher-end engineered precision components, while the remainder will support business growth, Tiwari said. CapGrid previously raised $5 Mn in an extended Series A round led by Anicut Growth Fund. Matching Suppliers With Orders Founded in 2021 by Tiwari and Himanshu Raghuvanshi, CapGrid serves original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) and Tier I suppliers across automotive, consumer durables, and heavy industries. It owns no factories. Instead, its cloud manufacturing platform coordinates component design, development, production, and delivery through third-party manufacturers. CapGrid says it uses AI and ML to match orders with suppliers and track production schedules and quality requirements. According to the startup, its supplier partners operate at around 60% capacity. CapGrid pools orders from different OEMs to put that spare capacity to use. Its supply chain control tower tracks sourcing, procurement, production, and deliveries, while 14 fulfilment centres across India’s major OEM clusters manage inventory and component deliveries to assembly lines. CapGrid also offers new product development, import localisation, and value engineering, helping customers develop parts, replace imports, and improve component designs and sourcing costs. Moving Beyond Automotive CapGrid initially focused on automotive, tapping manufacturers’ need to source components and manage suppliers. India’s auto component industry recorded turnover of ₹7.59 Lakh Cr in FY26, up 12.7%, according to ACMA. Supplies to OEMs increased 16.3% to ₹6.52 Lakh Cr. Having expanded beyond automotive, CapGrid now plans to enter drone manufacturing and data centres. Tiwari said operating revenue grew around 14% to ₹240 Cr in FY26, with ₹350 Cr targeted for FY27. Its annualised revenue run rate has risen from around ₹300 Cr six months ago to ₹360-370 Cr, with ₹500 Cr the next target. Inc42 Take: Can CapGrid Move Up The Manufacturing Value Chain? CapGrid’s next bet is to move beyond consolidating component procurement into higher-end engineered parts. Its existing OEM relationships and supplier network give it a base to build on, but spare factory capacity alone will not establish an advantage in more complex manufacturing. It will depend on the engineering expertise CapGrid brings to component development and production. The commercial question is whether this shift can improve the economics of its business. Operating revenue grew around 14% in FY26, while its FY27 target implies substantially faster growth. Entering drones and data centres could widen its customer base, but without margin and working-capital disclosures, it remains unclear whether more complex orders will translate into better returns.

india-deep-tech-e307fa0b9b.fulltext: Bengaluru-based Pixxel has set up a new subsidiary in the US, Pixxel Federal, to tap into the US government market and build on its existing engagements with NASA and the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO). The startup, which just raised $100 Mn last month, is now planning to set up an office around Washington, DC to work more closely with government customers and partners. The US subsidiary intends to offer earth observation technologies, satellite mission systems and geospatial intelligence to American government agencies across civilian, defence and intelligence sectors. “The US government market represents a significant opportunity for Pixxel as we expand our capabilities beyond hyperspectral imaging into advanced sensing technologies, software, and satellite systems,” said the startup’s founder and CEO Awais Ahmed. Pixxel executive Allyson Jenkins – previously Vice President, Public Sector – has been appointed CEO of Pixxel Federal. She had already been leading the company’s US government business since joining in January 2025. Important to mention that Pixxel recently secured a contract through NASA’s Commercial SmallSat Data Acquisition Programme and a Strategic Commercial Enhancements contract from the NRO. The new subsidiary will build on these relationships to pursue additional federal contracts and strengthen the company’s position in the US space and geospatial intelligence market. It will leverage Pixxel’s hyperspectral satellites, Earth intelligence software and satellite mission systems for applications such as camouflage detection, terrain characterisation, critical mineral and rare earth element detection, environmental monitoring and agriculture. Founded in 2019 by BITS Pilani alumni Ahmed and Kshitij Khandelwal, Pixxel claims to operate the world’s highest-resolution constellation of commercial hyperspectral satellites, which can capture light across a large number of narrow wavelength bands to identify details or changes on the Earth’s surface that conventional imagery may miss. Besides its US government contracts, Pixxel has won multiple iDEX challenges in India from the Ministry of Defence and is currently developing a public-private Earth observation satellite constellation under IN-SPACe. The proposed constellation, which is expected to be India’s first of its kind, will comprise 12 satellites carrying different types of imaging sensors. In September, the startup raised $100 Mn in a Series C round co-led by Temasek and Seraphim, marking the largest single investment round for an Indian spacetech company. With the round, Pixxel’s total private funding now is around $195 Mn. Investors like Google, Radical Ventures, growX ventures, Lightspeed Venture Partners, 360 ONE Asset, are on its cap table.

Apple’s long-awaited artificial intelligence features will be officially launched in China in December, ending two years of regulatory uncertainty as the US tech giant seeks to bring advanced technologies to its second-largest market with the help of Alibaba Group Holding.
The first batch of Apple Intelligence services will roll out to Chinese iPhone users alongside the iOS 27.3 update in December, following an open beta test with developers starting November 4, the US company said in a statement on Saturday.
The initial roll-out will include around 18 new features provided by Apple Intelligence, including writing tools for summarising and proofreading, live translation for phone calls and messages, as well as visual intelligence via camera controls, according to the statement.
However, Chinese users will not have the same access as those in many international markets, as Apple noted that its latest Siri AI capabilities and other next-generation AI services, launched by the company in September, would be excluded from this initial release. Siri is the virtual assistant across Apple’s ecosystem.
The statement did not specify when Apple Intelligence would be available to users of other Apple devices in China.
Notably, Alibaba’s flagship AI model Qwen will be integrated into Apple Intelligence through a partnership between the two firms that allows users to prompt Qwen for text generation, image creation, as well as photo or document analysis via Siri.
“We are delighted to cooperate with Apple,” said Eddie Wu Yongming, chief executive officer of Alibaba, in a statement on Saturday. “Qwen will draw on Alibaba’s deep AI technology stack to deeply integrate into the Apple ecosystem, jointly delivering entirely new intelligent experiences for Apple users in China.”
The launch came after Apple faced years of regulatory headwinds in bringing its AI services to its second-largest market. While Apple Intelligence was launched in the US and other international markets in 2024, China’s cyberspace rules require generative AI models deployed in the country to pass rigorous safety reviews by the country’s internet watchdog.
In July, Chinese regulators granted Apple the long-awaited licence to roll out AI services on iPhones in the country, alongside six other smartphone-based AI services, including those for Samsung Electronics and Huawei Technologies.

climate-energy-77080493f7.headline: COP17: Key outcomes agreed at the UN biodiversity conference in Yerevan
climate-energy-77080493f7.fulltext:
COP17: Key outcomes agreed at the UN biodiversity conference in Yerevan
Countries have completed the first “global review” of their progress towards reversing nature loss by 2030 at the COP17 biodiversity talks in Yerevan, Armenia.
The review “notes with deep concern” that, unless action is “rapidly accelerated”, the goal to reverse nature loss and meet a set of 23 targets by 2030 “will not be achieved”.
It “urges” countries to accelerate action, including by “increased ambition in addressing the gaps”.
Much of the discussions in Yerevan focused on how to raise the necessary funds to help developing countries protect nature.
Some major economies pushed to expand the range of nations that are expected to provide finance, with countries agreeing at the end of the two weeks of talks that non-donors that want to contribute can “signal interest” before COP18.
This came after developed countries failed to meet a target to significantly ramp up nature finance over the last few years.
It also came as a landmark fund agreed at COP16 in Colombia to pay communities for the genetic resources derived from nature stands nearly empty two years on.
The Yerevan talks marked the halfway point of the “Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework” (GBF), the “Paris Agreement for nature” first made in 2022 and due to be achieved by 2030.
During the nearly 12-hour-long final plenary, countries voted for Quito, Ecuador, to host the COP18 nature talks, which will be held in 2028.
Countries managed to sign off on all the major negotiation texts, marking a stark contrast to COP16, which ran so far over time that the Colombian presidency lost “quorum”, forcing talks to resume in Rome months later.
Below, Carbon Brief has detailed analysis of all of the key outcomes from COP17.
Formal negotiations
Finance
Finance, predictably, was at the heart of the discord and deadlock at the Yerevan talks.
At COP17, discussions on finance had to achieve several outcomes.
The first part – to take stock of biodiversity finance mobilised so far to meet the nature deal’s goals – fell under the global review.
As the global report noted, developed countries failed to meet their commitments to raise “at least $20bn a year by 2025” for nature. Delegates pointed to falling aid levels and a sharp 27% decline in environmental funding for the 2026-30 period.
The second part was to agree on how to mobilise resources for the next four years, to meet the GBF’s goals and targets.
Calls to “broaden the contributor base” of who pays to protect nature – and whether that should include emerging economies – became the most fraught element of the talks.
Eventually, countries agreed on what Switzerland described as a “super, mega-delicate” text. It hinged on major “political compromises”, with “no major winner or loser”, according to Kenya.
Per the decision, countries that want to be included on a list of developed country donors can “signal interest” through bilateral, confidential consultations before COP18 and every alternate COP after.
Finally, countries also agreed on criteria to shape and resource a new, permanent financial mechanism to protect nature after 2030.
However, this did not immediately take the form of a new fund under the COP that biodiverse countries have demanded since 2022, deferring the mechanism’s institutional structure to COP18.
Resource mobilisation discussions at the GBF’s halfway mark were supposed to agree on how to close the “biodiversity finance gap” and to “increase resources from all sources” to “at least” $200bn per year by 2030, as set out in target 19 of the GBF.
The talks were largely dominated by a push, led by the JUSCANZ bloc of developed countries, to “broaden the contributor base”. This could see emerging economies, such as Qatar, China, Saudi Arabia and India, being added to the list of countries that pay to protect nature.
Article 20 of the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD) states that developed countries “shall provide new and additional financial resources” to developing countries to meet the costs of implementing measures to protect nature.
The text states that other countries – including emerging economies – may “voluntarily assume” these obligations to pay. However, it adds that this list of developed countries “shall” be reviewed periodically and amended “if necessary”.
The list was last amended in 2006.
(See this “jargon buster” which explains the specific meaning and legal weight of various terms and verbs used in UN formal documents.)
Discussions around this fraught subject had reached a dead end at intersessional talks this year, but resurfaced in Yerevan.
The first “non-paper” had four different options for expanding the contributor base. These ranged from using the World Bank’s country income groups “as a proxy” to identify high-income countries, to commissioning a study on the impacts of being included on the list.
By 21 October, the number of options swelled to eight, including two from Saudi Arabia and one from Peru.
Some countries “expressed concern” that certain options were based on a CBD secretariat study on “what constitutes a developed country”, Earth Negotiations Bulletin reported.
By the end of the first week, it was clear that the finance deadlock would have to go into informal ministerial consultations for any consensus to emerge.
At a press conference on 28 October, Christopher O’Sullivan, Ireland’s nature minister and representing the EU delegation, told Carbon Brief:
“Our position isn’t that we want to pull back in terms of contributing…but it’s been 20 years since that list was added to, times have changed and there are new realities. We just simply want those new realities reflected. I don’t fully understand why there’s so much opposition to that.”
The EU chose not to comment on which countries it would like to see on that list.
Lim Li Ching from the Third World Network, meanwhile, called the push for others to “assume the obligations” of developed countries “sheer hypocrisy”, adding that any country could make a voluntary contribution. She told Carbon Brief:
“At a forum like the CBD, this linking of income status with finance does not take into account where historical and current responsibilities lie. If you want to generate more funding for biodiversity, let’s look at sovereign debt burdens and rules, which are inequitable for developing countries. But if you can fund wars, and provide resources for your defence industry, then you know where the priorities are.”
On 29 October – at a plenary meant to adopt final texts for the most contentious subjects – Norway’s Gaute Hanssen announced that resource-mobilisation discussions would go into a smaller “friends of the chair” meeting.
Facilitated by Carolina Caceres from Canada and Imèn Meliane from Tunisia, the meeting would discuss the most contentious elements of a draft decision that had swelled to 112 brackets, denoting areas of disagreement on specific details in the text.
While the meeting was open to all, countries that were called to be present included Brazil, Canada, Chile, China, the EU, Fiji, Norway, Russia, Switzerland, Saudi Arabia, South Africa and the UK.
At the same time, a “non-paper” text by finance and environment ministers laid out countries’ red lines and compromises.
At the end of COP17, countries welcomed a final compromise text, with Kenya thanking the “strong women” co-chairs who strove to strike a “delicate” balance.
China, Saudi Arabia, Switzerland and Fiji cautioned against any further interventions, with Brazil warning: “If we open this text, we will never close it again.”
While the final decision “recognises” that “contributions from more parties would improve the mobilisation” of biodiversity finance, it steered away from issuing criteria to expand the list of donor countries.
The text makes it clear that no additions to the list would be made without inviting and confidentially consulting with interested countries, to secure their explicit consent.
Instead, the CBD secretariat “invites” countries keen to be on the list and “assume the obligations” of developed countries to “signal interest” before COP18 and at every alternate COP thereafter.
At the same time, developing countries can contribute to meeting the GBF and biodiversity convention’s goals on a “voluntary basis”, with contributions not implying inclusion on the list.
A negotiator for China told Carbon Brief at the closing plenary:
“We welcome this balanced document. It was a very long discussion that has gone [on] since [2022 nature talks in] Nairobi. But actually this time, there were a lot of sensitive issues, [there were] a lot of critical things we didn’t open in the contact groups; it mainly went to the high-level discussion.”
The decision also establishes a financial mechanism for nature funding after 2030 under the governance of the COP, a key ask from developing countries.
However, it defers decisions on what form this mechanism would take – whether this would be a new fund or based on existing arrangements – until COP18.
Oscar Soria at the Common Initiative told Carbon Brief that the decision on the financial mechanism leaves things “very open”, with “no movement” towards a new fund or money and no upgrades to existing funding arrangements.
The text acknowledges the links between debt and biodiversity eight times, mentioning how debt-related instruments can be included in biodiversity plans, but does not go further.
“It is almost as if the debt studies they called for at COP16 didn’t happen,” said Soria, who had earlier flagged serious methodological issues with the first-ever COP-commissioned report on debt and biodiversity.
Global review
In Yerevan, countries agreed on the first stocktake of progress towards the 2030 nature targets – known as the “global review”.
The review was one of the keenly anticipated outcomes from COP17 and was seen as less controversial than some of the other major negotiation strands.
It was swiftly signed off by countries at the start of the final COP17 plenary, with just one last-minute addition.
The concept of carrying out a global review on “collective progress” was set out in the GBF and its underlying documents.
The details of how this review would be carried out were supposed to be agreed at COP16, but it was not discussed before the plenary in Cali was suspended for loss of “quorum”. It was instead adopted at the resumed COP16 negotiations in Rome in February 2025.
The global review was based largely on the findings of the global report and other information provided by countries.
The final text “welcomes” and also “notes with deep concern” the findings of the global report. It then homes in on various ways countries can increase their biodiversity action to get on track to meet the targets.
As of 19 October, when COP17 officially began, the non-paper contained 152 brackets, which indicate areas of disagreement in UN texts.
Smaller “contact group” discussions took place to try and reduce the number of brackets throughout the first week. This group was co-chaired by Sanne Kruid from the Netherlands and Sivendra Michael from Fiji.
A few days into the talks, Kruid told Carbon Brief that the progress on the global review was “relatively positive”, with countries “engaging quite well”.
One contentious section of the 11-page text was paragraph 15, which “urges” countries to accelerate implementation of nature targets, “including by increased ambition” in addressing key challenges.
Some developing countries were wary of including the word “ambition” in this section, arguing that higher ambition requires more nature finance, which is already falling “far short”.
Kirsty Leong, a policy expert at WWF, told Carbon Brief:
“You have one side wanting to have very strong language and high ambition in what countries should do…and the other side of the room saying the main problem in implementation is that they don’t have the means to do it.”

health-tech-ebefed38fc.headline: Anthropic's next big AI business is life sciences, from biotech research to drug discovery
health-tech-ebefed38fc.fulltext:
Anthropic conquered coding. Now it's setting its sights on the human body.
Anthropic's S-1 filing, which outlines its ambitions and financials ahead of a massive initial public offering next month, reads as a life-sciences manifesto. The maker of Claude sees itself as a crucial cog in the next generation of biological and medicinal research — and is selling that lucrative vision to its would-be investors.
Anthropic is hoping for a wave of new discoveries that will support its do-gooder mission and convince the public of AI's power and worth. Its life-science focus could also support financial growth beyond its AI software engineering tools. It would promote the use of Anthropic's most advanced, expensive models in an industry already accustomed to spending billions on research and development.
The S-1 filing is scattered with references to biotech ambition. Its second line says AI "could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation" and "bring cures for major diseases within reach." A page later, biological progress tops the company's list of ways it hopes AI will improve lives.
Anthropic also references its life sciences business in its "growth strategy" section and writes that nine of the 10 largest pharmaceutical companies and eight of the 10 largest healthcare companies in the Fortune 500 spent at least $100,000 with Anthropic over a recent yearlong period.
"In the life sciences sector, where annual global pharmaceutical spend is expected to exceed $2 trillion in 2026, Claude is used in drug discovery and development by our customers, our biotechnology partners, and our own researchers," the company writes in the filing.
Anthropic declined to comment.
Anthropic has begun investing in life sciences
Anthropic has already gotten to work investing in life sciences. The company's Claude Science product, which is in beta, came out in June. OpenAI, Anthropic's erstwhile rival, has a competing offering dubbed Rosalind, while Google spinoff Isomorphic Labs plans to use AI to create cancer-beating drugs — promising a struggle between companies for research customers.
Besides that, Anthropic started a molecular biology lab in the Bay Area this year and spent $400 million in stock in April to buy the biotech startup Coefficient Bio. Vas Narasimhan, the CEO of the pharmaceutical company Novartis, also joined Anthropic's board in April. In August, Anthropic announced a new robotics standard that allows AI to control lab equipment. 
The company's careers page shows it's on a hiring spree for life sciences roles across chemistry, experimental biology, research engineering, and more. Two new roles opened late this week, offering $320,000 salaries to researchers capable of designing and manufacturing antibodies.
In its S-1, Anthropic touted its work with pharma giant Lilly, saying the $1.3 trillion company has 50,000 employees with access to a Claude enterprise account and that more than 85% of its staff actively use the tool.
CEO Dario Amodei is prioritizing life sciences
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, a former theoretical physicist, has repeatedly touted AI's potential in the life sciences as a reason to advance the tech's capabilities.
In a September essay about "pacing" AI research, Amodei said he had survived a cancer that wouldn't have been treatable in the 1970s, and his father had died of a disease cured shortly after his death.
He previously elaborated on the themes in a 2024 essay dubbed "Machines of Loving Grace."
"Biology is probably the area where scientific progress has the greatest potential to directly and unambiguously improve the quality of human life," Amodei wrote, adding that he hopes AI-enabled research will help prevent and treat all infectious diseases, eliminate most cancers, and double the human lifespan.
The general public is less optimistic. Anthropic recently published survey results from August, finding that 91% of staff think AI will make a Nobel-level discovery by 2030, compared with 39% of US adults. No AI-designed drugs have ever received FDA approval.
Ben Mann, the co-leader of Anthropic's Labs organization, which builds new products and created Claude Code, told Business Insider this August that his small team is also focusing more on life sciences.
"Labs itself has shifted its focus from sort of more standard software engineering things to things like what Dario has described as curing all diseases like, Machines of Loving Grace-style," Mann said.

health-tech-80014367ba.headline: India's Pharma Exports Rise 4.9% to $16.14 Billion in H1 FY27 as Europe, ASEAN Offset Softer US Shipments
health-tech-80014367ba.fulltext:
India’s pharmaceutical exporters added roughly three-quarters of a billion dollars in overseas sales in the first half of 2026-27, and the growth came from almost everywhere except the industry’s single largest market. Data released on 29 October by the Pharmaceuticals Export Promotion Council of India (Pharmexcil) put exports for April–September 2026 at USD 16.14 billion, up 4.90% from USD 15.38 billion in the same period of FY26.
The numbers at a glance
- H1 FY27 exports: USD 16.14 billion, up 4.90% year on year.
- Q2 FY27 (July–September): USD 8.04 billion, up 3.05% from USD 7.80 billion a year earlier.
- September 2026: USD 2,744.05 million, the highest monthly figure of the half-year and 4.68% above September 2025.
- Europe: USD 3.29 billion, up 9.66%, now 20.38% of total pharma exports.
Europe, ASEAN and Latin America carry the momentum
Within Europe, shipments to Germany grew 21.57%, while the Netherlands and France rose 15.93% and 15.02% respectively. Beyond Europe, exports to ASEAN countries climbed 21.54%, Latin America and the Caribbean recorded 16.58% growth and Africa grew 6.48%.
Pharmexcil did not publish a figure for the United States, but said shipments to that market moderated during the period, making the broader geographic spread the main reason overall exports kept growing. Industry observers quoted by ET Pharma linked the European gains to governments seeking to contain healthcare spending by switching from expensive brands to lower-cost generics and biosimilars through public procurement, which has helped Indian companies partly offset pricing pressure in the US.
Bulk drugs outpace formulations
Drug formulations and biologicals remained the backbone of the export basket at 73.84% of shipments, growing 3.81% year on year. The faster-moving segment was bulk drugs and drug intermediates, up 12.07%, while surgical product exports increased 9.53%. For India’s API and intermediates makers, the double-digit rise is a sign that overseas demand for Indian-made starting materials and ingredients continues to build.
Headwinds remain
The gains came despite continued supply-chain pressure linked to the prolonged West Asia crisis. According to industry executives cited by ET Pharma, many listed drugmakers are absorbing a margin hit of around 100–120 basis points from elevated solvent and crude oil prices.
Moving up the value chain
Pharmexcil Chairman Namit Joshi said India’s global reputation has been built on quality, affordable medicines and large-scale manufacturing, but the next phase should see Indian companies become “active partners in pharmaceutical innovation” rather than suppliers alone. “This will require greater investment in research and development, technology transfer and co-development of complex generics, biosimilars and specialised therapies,” he said, adding that Europe’s research ecosystem offers significant scope for such collaborations.
Vice Chairman Bhavin Mehta said the double-digit growth in bulk drugs and intermediates reflects the breadth of India’s manufacturing capability, and that continued investment in quality systems, advanced manufacturing and regulatory preparedness can help more exporters, including MSMEs, participate globally. The council said it will keep working with the government, industry and overseas regulators to strengthen market access and regulatory cooperation.
Why it matters
The half-year data reinforces a trend visible in several Q2 FY27 company results: Indian drugmakers are leaning harder on Europe, emerging markets and API supply to balance a softer, price-pressured US generics business. With formulation growth in low single digits, the push towards complex generics, biosimilars and higher-value products that Pharmexcil is urging may decide how quickly that diversification turns into faster export growth.
