india-77e4ef7de5.headline: Scotch prices row: India-UK trade deal faces big test as govt calls liquor giants for talks
india-77e4ef7de5.fulltext:
NEW DELHI: The commerce ministry is set to meet representatives of domestic and international liquor companies on Monday as a dispute over import duties on Scotch whisky threatens to complicate the recently implemented India-UK free trade agreement.
The disagreement centres on whether Scotch whisky imported in large quantities for use in domestic manufacturing should receive the same tariff benefits as whisky brought into the country in finished bottles.
Under the trade agreement, which came into force in July, India agreed to reduce import duties on certain Scotch whisky products from 150% to 75%.
However, the authorities have told major liquor companies that bulk Scotch imports do not qualify for the lower rate.
The decision has triggered objections from global spirits companies Diageo and Pernod Ricard, as well as domestic liquor manufacturers, who argue that excluding bulk imports could undermine the benefits of the trade deal.
Manufacturers flag concerns over domestic industry
The Confederation of Indian Alcoholic Beverage Companies (CIABC), which represents several major domestic liquor manufacturers, has urged the government to reconsider its position, according to a confidential letter dated October 27 and reviewed by news agency Reuters.
The industry body warned that denying the lower tariff to bulk Scotch could make it more attractive for companies to import finished whisky from Britain rather than bring in the spirit in bulk and manufacture or bottle products in India.
"Such an outcome would run counter to the objective of strengthening domestic manufacturing under Make in India," the letter said, calling for urgent government intervention to prevent disruptions.
The CIABC's members include listed companies such as Radico Khaitan, which makes 8PM whisky, and Allied Blenders and Distillers, the maker of Officer's Choice.
Allied Blenders said in an investor presentation this week that it is “one of the largest bulk Scotch importers” and that the UK trade agreement would improve its “luxury portfolio accessibility”.
Around 80% of Scotch whisky imported from Britain by volume arrives in bulk and is used in the production of popular brands in India. The country's $65 billion alcoholic beverages industry had expected the reduction in import duties to support business.
Diageo and Pernod Ricard also raise objections
The International Spirits & Wines Association of India, which represents companies including Diageo and Pernod Ricard, has privately cautioned New Delhi that excluding bulk Scotch from the tariff concession could undermine the trade agreement.
The two companies have commercial interests in India's spirits market, where imported Scotch is used both in finished products and in domestic manufacturing.
The CIABC's intervention has widened the dispute, bringing domestic manufacturers into the same debate as major international spirits companies.
The companies and industry bodies did not respond to Reuters' requests for comment. All the firms have said they comply with the law.
Dispute puts trade agreement under scrutiny
Senior Commerce Ministry officials are expected to hold closed-door discussions with executives from domestic and foreign liquor companies on Monday, according to four people familiar with the matter.
The ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment outside regular business hours on Saturday.
The dispute marks the first major disagreement linked to the India-UK trade agreement, following years of negotiations in which tariffs on Scotch whisky were a key sticking point.
Britain has said it is working with India to resolve the issue, while the Scottish government has also raised concerns with New Delhi over the treatment of bulk Scotch imports, news agency Reuters had previously reported.

india-ac4113432a.headline: How Ambani’s Jio became India’s second-largest company
india-ac4113432a.fulltext:
How Ambani’s Jio became India’s second-largest company
Mukesh Ambani’s Jio upended India’s telecoms market with free data and crushed its competition. Now, it has made India’s largest-ever stock market debut.
New Delhi, India – This week, Mumbai, India’s financial capital, was the site of a splashy display by Asia’s richest man, Mukesh Ambani, with DJ sets, a drone show and a jam session with popular Indian singers.
The festivities marked India’s largest-ever initial public offering (IPO), as Ambani’s Jio Platforms raised $3.2bn in its stock market debut.
The telecoms-to-digital company’s shares surged by a whopping 21 percent on Wednesday, valuing the company at $131.5bn and making it the country’s second most valuable, only behind its parent, Ambani’s Reliance Industries.
The Ambani family’s Jio Platforms counts global tech giants Meta and Google among its major shareholders, following their multibillion-dollar investments in the company in 2020 – and serves more than 530 million customers.
“Jio may not be visible. But it pulses through every digital dream of India,” said Anant Ambani, the family’s youngest son, who is an additional director on the company’s board, at the celebratory event. “Today, Jio is shared with India.”
So, how did Ambani’s Jio disrupt one of the world’s most competitive telecoms markets – and in the process, help consolidate it into what some observers describe as an oligopoly?
What is Jio, and who is Ambani?
Mukesh Ambani is the richest man in Asia, according to Forbes magazine, with a net worth of $80bn.
In the world’s most populous country – with more than one billion people – some say it is no exaggeration to call India “Ambani’s world”.
Since inheriting Reliance Industries from his father, Mukesh Ambani, 69, has expanded the conglomerate far beyond its textile and petrochemical roots.
From food and clothes to fuel, the internet and streaming, the reach of the Ambani family’s business empire extends into nearly every facet of daily life in India.
In October, United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio travelled to India for a two-day visit, during which he toured the Jamnagar refinery complex in Gujarat, owned by Ambani’s Reliance Industries. Rubio did not visit New Delhi on that trip and officials were angered by suggestions that ministers should travel to see him instead.
How did Jio become India’s largest telecoms operator?
In 2016, while American consumers were paying an average of about $7 per gigabyte of mobile data, Reliance entered the scene in India with Jio, upending one of the biggest telecommunication markets by size, by offering data free for months.
Jio crossed 100 million subscribers in its first 170 days in business, a milestone described at the time as the fastest achieved by a mobile operator globally. Those days were notable for the long queues in front of pop-up tents in Indian cities, giving away SIM cards.
But entry barriers into India’s then diverse telecom market were also high. Jio’s entry required a total investment commitment of nearly $22.48bn in September 2016, spent on spectrum acquisition, network infrastructure and fibre backhaul.
Backed by Reliance’s deep pockets, Jio’s arrival fundamentally changed India’s telecoms market – prepping itself to absorb initial losses in operations in exchange for the prize of accumulating millions of customers.
Competitors were forced to slash their prices sharply, consumption surged and millions of Indians began accessing the internet on their smartphones.
In just three years, Jio had become India’s largest telecom operator by subscriber numbers. In the coming years, Ambani expanded Jio into a digital ecosystem including JioCinema and entertainment for streaming and sporting events, and JioCloud for cloud storage and digital services.
What has been the cost of Jio’s rise?
Since 2016, when Jio was launched, Ambani’s fortune has grown nearly 3.8 times – with increase of approximately $60bn.
Jio’s entry triggered a 42.8 percent decline in India’s average telecom revenues per subscriber, from nearly $1.32 in 2016 to $0.75 in 2019, according to a research paper published in ScienceDirect.
The researchers believe the scale of this price decline was unprecedented and left India with a highly concentrated telecom market.
In the meantime, seven of the 10 incumbent operators exited the market either due to bankruptcy or merger, notably Aircel, Videocon, Telenor India, Tata Teleservices and Reliance Communications.
Reliance Communications, founded by Anil Ambani, Mukesh’s younger brother, suffered severe financial losses and filed for bankruptcy in 2019. The brothers, once joint heirs to their father’s business empire, have had a long and bitter falling-out over the division of the Reliance conglomerate following his death in 2002, with their rivalry playing out for years.
Today, Jio and Airtel have strengthened their positions, while Vodafone Idea continues to face financial difficulties. These three operators control more than 92 percent of India’s telecoms market.
Researchers found that while consumers benefitted from cheap services during the price war, those benefits declined after the market reconsolidated.
In July 2024, Jio introduced price increases of approximately 12 to 25 percent across plans and other telecom operators followed suit, also raising tariffs substantially.
In its IPO disclosures, Jio has noted that further tariff increases may not necessarily translate into higher revenues because consumers could downgrade plans or switch operators.
What will Jio and Ambani do next?
Jio is considering deploying a low-Earth-orbit satellite to deliver internet services from space, a venture that would put it in direct competition with Elon Musk’s Starlink, which has been seeking regulatory approval to enter India for years.
Reliance Group has also invested in the United States. Last month, Ambani took State Secretary Marco Rubio to tour the largest oil refinery at the Jamnagar facility, where both discussed processing more Venezuelan oil.
Musk, the world’s richest man and also a key ally of US President Donald Trump, recently hit out at Ambani.
His Starlink space telecommunications firm has struggled for years to secure a licence to operate in India.
In a series of X posts, Musk accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government of stalling Starlink’s entry to favour market leader Ambani’s telecom firm, Jio.
Musk taunted Ambani directly, addressing him as “Prime Minister Ambani” and asking whether he would “consider allowing Starlink to compete”. Starlink, Musk wrote, was being blocked by “oligarchs” protecting their “monopolistic chokehold” on Indians.
In a statement issued on X, Reliance said it has “never feared competition” and has “grown in an India that welcomes investment and innovation, homegrown or international”.

work-careers-2da797d2bc.headline: H-1B Visas, Green Cards: What Indian Professionals Should Watch After US Midterms
work-careers-2da797d2bc.fulltext:
A Democratic victory could increase congressional scrutiny of immigration rules and put some Republican-backed proposals on hold.
The H-1B programme allows US employers to hire foreign professionals for jobs requiring specialised skills.
The US midterm elections in November could influence the country's H-1B visa programme and employment-based green card policies, as Democrats seek to challenge President Donald Trump's immigration agenda.
A Democratic victory could increase congressional scrutiny of immigration rules and put some Republican-backed proposals on hold, although major policy changes are unlikely, according to an ICICI Bank research report.
Republicans currently control both the House of Representatives and the Senate. However, Democrats are expected to make gains in the November 2026 elections.
Market estimates cited in the report put the probability of Democrats winning both chambers at 63%, while the likelihood of the party winning only the House stands at 29%.
The outcome will determine how much room Congress has to influence immigration policy during the remainder of Trump's term. However, even if Democrats take control of both chambers, the President will retain the power to veto legislation, making major changes difficult.
The H-1B programme allows US employers to hire foreign professionals for jobs requiring specialised skills. It is widely used by technology companies and IT services firms that recruit workers from countries such as India.
Republicans have proposed legislation that could tighten requirements for employers hiring foreign workers. The Protecting American Workers Through H-1B Modernization Act proposes higher wage thresholds for certain H-1B exemptions.
Another proposal, the H-1B Visa Fraud Crackdown Act, seeks stricter penalties for violations of the programme.
If passed, these measures could increase hiring and compliance costs for US companies, particularly IT services firms that rely on foreign professionals.
A Democratic-controlled Congress could make it harder for such proposals to advance. Democrats have also introduced measures dealing with domestic visa renewals and greater transparency in the Department of Homeland Security's enforcement activities.
Employment-based green cards are another area to watch. The proposed SMARTER Act seeks to replace the existing employment-based immigration framework with a skills-based points system. It also proposes narrowing family-sponsored immigration and eliminating the Diversity Visa programme.
For Indian professionals seeking permanent residency in the US, a shift to a points-based system could change how applicants qualify for employment-based green cards. The eventual impact would depend on the selection criteria and transition arrangements if the proposal is enacted.
Democrats, meanwhile, have called for preserving and expanding legal immigration pathways. Their proposals include measures aimed at creating more pathways to citizenship.
However, these remain legislative proposals and would not automatically change existing immigration rules.
A change in congressional control is unlikely to bring an immediate reversal of the Trump administration's immigration policies.
The Republican-controlled Congress has already approved $70 billion in funding for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and Border Patrol for the remainder of Trump's term.
This limits the scope for an incoming Democratic Congress to immediately alter immigration enforcement through funding restrictions.
According to ICICI Bank, a Democratic victory could increase oversight of immigration agencies, delay restrictive proposals and provide greater support for legislation expanding legal immigration pathways. However, the extent of these changes would depend on congressional approval and the administration's response.
For Indian professionals, the key issues to watch are proposed changes to H-1B wage requirements, employer compliance rules, employment-based green card eligibility and visa renewal procedures.
The midterm elections could influence the direction of US immigration policy, but any change to the existing system will depend on whether proposed legislation can clear Congress and receive presidential approval.

world-92c9aea9fb.headline: Disquiet grows in Albanese’s back yard as Grayndler artists unite against ‘insane’ AI proposal
world-92c9aea9fb.fulltext:
The prime minister is facing growing discontent within his own electorate as creatives push back against the federal government’s proposal to allow AI companies to scrape everything Australians create online.
Anthony Albanese’s seat of Grayndler in Sydney’s inner west is home to more than 3,000 cultural and creative businesses, and 10% of its workers are employed in cultural and creative fields – compared with 4.2% nationally.
He has held it on a safe margin for three decades, and has spoken of its high representation of live music, theatre and artist spaces with pride.
But now, as Labor considers giving AI companies access to Australian creatives’ works by default as it pursues a compromise with US tech giants, locals are reacting with dismay.
Labor is mulling over the copyright changes in a suite of reforms surrounding AI, including datacentres, energy and the economy. While Albanese has promised “the strongest possible protection”, warning it would be “theft” if creatives weren’t paid for their work, creative industries are alarmed that AI companies have requested a weakening of copyright law to train their models using Australian material.
Some AI companies have said making licensing agreements under existing copyright law would be too difficult, while Anthropic suggested an “opt-out” model which would allow it to scrape content unless a rightholder objected, prompting warnings from Coalition senators and the recording industry that this could amount to an acquisition of property by the government.
The federal government’s draft laws are expected by the end of the year, with consideration in parliament due in 2027.
Pete Strong is a screenprinter and Greens councillor for Bayside. His business is based in Grayndler, with his solar-powered wheelie bin sound systems a fixture around the inner west.
He said AI could be “good for humanity” but is now an “extraction industry mining for profit for the few”.
“I’m completely against [the federal government’s proposal],” he said.
“There’s obviously an AI gold rush at the moment, it’s the wild west and we really need to push back. It’s hard enough being a starving artist these days without having all your work taken and used in these nefarious ways.”
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
This year Strong curated a show called “overthrow the algorithm”. He has also been a vocal critic of a proposed datacentre at Cooks Cove.
“I’ve seen a backlash [to the government] already,” he said. “It started with the datacentre uprising.”
Labor’s proposals were leaked in September as senior personnel from OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, met Labor ministers and warned that Australia’s copyright laws were preventing the company from training models locally.
For the inner west designer and artist Lu Campbell-Smith, AI has been useful in her practice. But she said having to opt out was “outrageous”.
“It just really pinpoints how Australia’s [a] test market and they’re happy for us to just be a little resource to be exploited,” she said.
“Why would anyone want to make anything and post anything online if … you’re creating free content for an AI machine?”
Grayndler has always been an ultra-safe Labor seat. Albanese’s face as a much younger man is plastered on to cans of Albo Pale Ale at Willie the Boatman brewery in St Peters. For the past few elections, he has won on first preferences alone.
But at the next federal election, he will be challenged by 28-year-old Hannah Ferguson, the co-founder of Cheek Media, who will run as an independent.
No sitting member has lost their seat from such a margin at a federal election. Were it not for the longstanding popularity of Albanese, Grayndler would have been a prime target for the Greens and progressive independents.
Now, Ferguson is betting that his popularity is waning. And polling indicates the same. Guardian Australia’s latest Essential poll shows Albanese’s disapproval rating at 56%, the equal highest since he took office.
At Tortuga Studios and the aerie, one of the longest-running artist-led spaces in Sydney which operates out of an old brick factory in St Peters, the frustration is palpable.
H Morgan-Harris, an author, curator and director of the space, said there was a risk the Australian creative ecosystem could be “decimated”.
“This whole conversation always comes back to money,” she said, adding: “The artistic ecosystem is the bedrock of human interaction and human connection. And you risk our societal value by threatening it.”
Morgan-Harris’s copywriting industry has already been “heavily impacted” by AI, she said. Asked what her response was to the federal government’s latest proposal, she said it wasn’t “one you can print”.
“I just feel like artists are the first to be thrown under the bus,” she said.
“I think a lot of people were really excited when [Albanese] got into government, but there’s a yawning chasm in terms of the recognition, consideration and protection of the value of this sector. This honestly feels like the end of times to a lot of us.”
Jason Zoidberg, a co-founder of Monster Mouse Studios in Marrickville, said the AI industry had already “without consequence” stolen the “collective labour” uploaded by artists. He said it was “utterly crazy” that the government was considering giving companies the green light to do so.
“It just feels insane that they’re like, ‘Yeah, please come and we want to invest in you,’ when we’ve seen all these horrible things that they’re doing,” he said.
If there is a flipside, Zoidberg said, he is witnessing a surge in interest in traditional, hands-on art forms.
“There’s a backlash in the inner west against social media and AI,” Zoidberg said. “So our workshops are actually getting more participants. But it is also just a niche, a little inner west bubble.”

health-tech-6b30c0c0f2.headline: India’s Pharma Exports Grow 4.9 Percent to $16.14 Billion in H1 FY27
health-tech-6b30c0c0f2.fulltext:
India’s pharmaceutical exports increased nearly 5% to ₹1.53 lakh crore (US$16.13 billion) during the first half of FY27, according to data released by the Pharmaceuticals Export Promotion Council of India (Pharmexcil). Strong demand from Europe, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and Latin America supported this growth. During the second quarter of FY27, pharmaceutical exports rose 3.05% to ₹76,145.73 crore (US$8.04 billion). Meanwhile, September recorded the highest monthly export value of ₹25,988.52 crore (US$2.74 billion), registering 4.68% year-on-year (YoY) growth.
Europe Leads Growth in Pharmaceutical Exports
Europe emerged as a major growth market for Indian pharmaceutical products. Exports to the region increased 9.66% to ₹31,142.75 crore (US$3.29 billion), accounting for 20.38% of India’s total pharmaceutical exports. Similarly, shipments to ASEAN markets recorded strong growth of 21.54%, while exports to Latin America and the Caribbean increased 16.58%. Africa also registered a 6.48% rise in pharmaceutical imports from India. These gains across key international markets helped sustain overall export growth.
Drug Formulations and Bulk Drugs Drive Export Performance
Drug formulations and biologicals remained the largest export category, contributing 73.84% of India’s total pharmaceutical shipments and recording 3.81% growth. Additionally, bulk drugs and drug intermediates registered a stronger increase of 12.07%, while surgical exports grew 9.53%. The performance highlights the growing contribution of India’s pharmaceutical manufacturing capabilities across multiple product segments.
Pharmexcil Highlights Opportunities in High-Value Medicines
Commenting on the export performance, Pharmexcil Chairman Namit Joshi said India has established a strong global reputation for quality, affordable medicines and large-scale manufacturing. However, he emphasised that the next phase of growth must focus on moving up the pharmaceutical value chain. He identified Europe as a significant opportunity for Indian companies to expand into the co-development of complex generics, biosimilars and specialised therapies. As reported by ibef.org, Pharmexcil Vice Chairman Bhavin Mehta said the double-digit growth in bulk drugs and intermediates reflects the strength and diversity of India’s domestic pharmaceutical manufacturing capabilities. He also emphasised that continued investment in quality systems will help Indian pharmaceutical exporters strengthen their global presence and participate in higher-value international markets.

According to data released by the Pharmaceuticals Export Promotion Council of India (Pharmexcil), the first-half performance saw growth across drug formulations and biologicals, bulk drugs and drug intermediates, and surgical products.

Region-wise, exports to Europe rose 9.66 per cent to USD 3,288.27 million, making up 20.38 per cent -- or over one-fifth -- of India's total pharmaceutical exports during H1 FY27.
Exports to the ASEAN region grew 21.54 per cent, Latin America and the Caribbean rose 16.58 per cent, and shipments to Africa increased 6.48 per cent. These diversified geographic gains helped sustain overall export growth even as shipments to the US moderated during the period, Pharmexcil said.

The FBI blamed North Korea for the $6.3 billion Binance hack as the exchange replaced 90% of stolen funds.
The FBI has blamed North Korea for the theft of $6.3 billion in cryptocurrency from Binance, calling it the work of a state-backed hacking group known as TraderTraitor. The attack, described as the biggest crypto heist in history, took place on Thursday and affected the world's largest cryptocurrency exchange.
Binance said on Saturday that it had replaced 90% of the stolen assets using company funds and would cover the remaining losses. Co-CEO Richard Teng assured customers that they would not face any financial impact from the breach.
In a statement, the FBI linked the attack to TraderTraitor, a group previously blamed for a $1.5 billion hack of cryptocurrency exchange Bybit last year. The bureau described the latest incident as part of the group's malicious cyber activity.
FBI warns of attempts to move stolen cryptocurrency
Deep Dive
The FBI said its investigation found that the hackers had started converting the stolen funds, mainly into Ethereum, another major cryptocurrency.
The bureau warned that the group could use decentralised finance (DeFi) platforms and instant swap services to move the assets and make them harder to trace.
It also urged cryptocurrency exchanges, blockchain tracking firms and other organisations to block transactions connected to wallet addresses identified in the investigation. The move is aimed at preventing the stolen funds from being laundered.

Binance said it had recovered or replaced 90% of the stolen amount by purchasing new tokens with company money. The remaining 10% involves less liquid cryptocurrencies, which may take longer to replace.
"We've now replenished 90% of the stolen assets, and we're committed to covering the remaining 10%. Our users will not bear the financial impact of this incident," Teng wrote on X.

beyond-your-beat-ac4113432a.headline: How Ambani’s Jio became India’s second-largest company
beyond-your-beat-ac4113432a.fulltext:
How Ambani’s Jio became India’s second-largest company
Mukesh Ambani’s Jio upended India’s telecoms market with free data and crushed its competition. Now, it has made India’s largest-ever stock market debut.
New Delhi, India – This week, Mumbai, India’s financial capital, was the site of a splashy display by Asia’s richest man, Mukesh Ambani, with DJ sets, a drone show and a jam session with popular Indian singers.
The festivities marked India’s largest-ever initial public offering (IPO), as Ambani’s Jio Platforms raised $3.2bn in its stock market debut.
The telecoms-to-digital company’s shares surged by a whopping 21 percent on Wednesday, valuing the company at $131.5bn and making it the country’s second most valuable, only behind its parent, Ambani’s Reliance Industries.
The Ambani family’s Jio Platforms counts global tech giants Meta and Google among its major shareholders, following their multibillion-dollar investments in the company in 2020 – and serves more than 530 million customers.
“Jio may not be visible. But it pulses through every digital dream of India,” said Anant Ambani, the family’s youngest son, who is an additional director on the company’s board, at the celebratory event. “Today, Jio is shared with India.”
So, how did Ambani’s Jio disrupt one of the world’s most competitive telecoms markets – and in the process, help consolidate it into what some observers describe as an oligopoly?
What is Jio, and who is Ambani?
Mukesh Ambani is the richest man in Asia, according to Forbes magazine, with a net worth of $80bn.
In the world’s most populous country – with more than one billion people – some say it is no exaggeration to call India “Ambani’s world”.
Since inheriting Reliance Industries from his father, Mukesh Ambani, 69, has expanded the conglomerate far beyond its textile and petrochemical roots.
From food and clothes to fuel, the internet and streaming, the reach of the Ambani family’s business empire extends into nearly every facet of daily life in India.
In October, United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio travelled to India for a two-day visit, during which he toured the Jamnagar refinery complex in Gujarat, owned by Ambani’s Reliance Industries. Rubio did not visit New Delhi on that trip and officials were angered by suggestions that ministers should travel to see him instead.
How did Jio become India’s largest telecoms operator?
In 2016, while American consumers were paying an average of about $7 per gigabyte of mobile data, Reliance entered the scene in India with Jio, upending one of the biggest telecommunication markets by size, by offering data free for months.
Jio crossed 100 million subscribers in its first 170 days in business, a milestone described at the time as the fastest achieved by a mobile operator globally. Those days were notable for the long queues in front of pop-up tents in Indian cities, giving away SIM cards.
But entry barriers into India’s then diverse telecom market were also high. Jio’s entry required a total investment commitment of nearly $22.48bn in September 2016, spent on spectrum acquisition, network infrastructure and fibre backhaul.
Backed by Reliance’s deep pockets, Jio’s arrival fundamentally changed India’s telecoms market – prepping itself to absorb initial losses in operations in exchange for the prize of accumulating millions of customers.
Competitors were forced to slash their prices sharply, consumption surged and millions of Indians began accessing the internet on their smartphones.
In just three years, Jio had become India’s largest telecom operator by subscriber numbers. In the coming years, Ambani expanded Jio into a digital ecosystem including JioCinema and entertainment for streaming and sporting events, and JioCloud for cloud storage and digital services.
What has been the cost of Jio’s rise?
Since 2016, when Jio was launched, Ambani’s fortune has grown nearly 3.8 times – with increase of approximately $60bn.
Jio’s entry triggered a 42.8 percent decline in India’s average telecom revenues per subscriber, from nearly $1.32 in 2016 to $0.75 in 2019, according to a research paper published in ScienceDirect.
The researchers believe the scale of this price decline was unprecedented and left India with a highly concentrated telecom market.
In the meantime, seven of the 10 incumbent operators exited the market either due to bankruptcy or merger, notably Aircel, Videocon, Telenor India, Tata Teleservices and Reliance Communications.
Reliance Communications, founded by Anil Ambani, Mukesh’s younger brother, suffered severe financial losses and filed for bankruptcy in 2019. The brothers, once joint heirs to their father’s business empire, have had a long and bitter falling-out over the division of the Reliance conglomerate following his death in 2002, with their rivalry playing out for years.
Today, Jio and Airtel have strengthened their positions, while Vodafone Idea continues to face financial difficulties. These three operators control more than 92 percent of India’s telecoms market.
Researchers found that while consumers benefitted from cheap services during the price war, those benefits declined after the market reconsolidated.
In July 2024, Jio introduced price increases of approximately 12 to 25 percent across plans and other telecom operators followed suit, also raising tariffs substantially.
In its IPO disclosures, Jio has noted that further tariff increases may not necessarily translate into higher revenues because consumers could downgrade plans or switch operators.
What will Jio and Ambani do next?
Jio is considering deploying a low-Earth-orbit satellite to deliver internet services from space, a venture that would put it in direct competition with Elon Musk’s Starlink, which has been seeking regulatory approval to enter India for years.
Reliance Group has also invested in the United States. Last month, Ambani took State Secretary Marco Rubio to tour the largest oil refinery at the Jamnagar facility, where both discussed processing more Venezuelan oil.
Musk, the world’s richest man and also a key ally of US President Donald Trump, recently hit out at Ambani.
His Starlink space telecommunications firm has struggled for years to secure a licence to operate in India.
In a series of X posts, Musk accused Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government of stalling Starlink’s entry to favour market leader Ambani’s telecom firm, Jio.
Musk taunted Ambani directly, addressing him as “Prime Minister Ambani” and asking whether he would “consider allowing Starlink to compete”. Starlink, Musk wrote, was being blocked by “oligarchs” protecting their “monopolistic chokehold” on Indians.
In a statement issued on X, Reliance said it has “never feared competition” and has “grown in an India that welcomes investment and innovation, homegrown or international”.

ai-8f5ebd02c3.fulltext:
OpenAI’s latest funding round isn’t quite living up to expectations, according to multiple news reports.
OpenAI was previously reported to be raising $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation, and then at a $1.25 trillion valuation, ahead of a planned IPO. But The Financial Times reported Friday that the company has subsequently lowered its funding target to $20 billion, with a first close that’s expected to be even lower than that.
The round will be led by a group of investors from the United Arab Emirates, the FT said. A subsequent retail offering for wealthy individuals could bring the total funding amount to the $20 billion target.
A follow-up story in The Wall Street Journal offered more details, namely that the company has secured $11 billion so far, and that its fundraising efforts had met with a “tepid” response from some large investors.
TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment. The company’s reported funding challenges could be blamed, in part, on bad timing, as Wall Street investors have become wary of heavy AI infrastructure spending, leading to a major sell off of tech stocks. And Anthropic’s planned IPO could be facing challenges, too.
